title: Layerwise quant triage - onprem latency, KV & batching
summary: Deep technical triage on observed accuracy regressions after mixed INT8/GPTQ conversion on-prem. Focus: layerwise errors, KV cache interaction, batching/latency tradeoffs, and a plan for targeted benchmarks and temporary mitigations. SE proposed per-layer mixed precision and runtime fallback; customer to run targeted evals and share trace logs.
topics: INT8 vs AWQ vs GPTQ tradeoffs
KV cache and prefix caching behavior
Batching impact on latency and p95/p99
action_items: Evan: produce per-layer accuracy delta table from recent GPTQ job and upload to shared S3 (due 2025-10-17)
Samir: share model conversion command line and quantization config used for the last run (due 2025-10-16)
Tess: run the Redwood provided benchmark script on the onprem cluster (dedicated pool) with 1,2,4 batch sizes and attach logs (due 2025-10-20)
Priya: send security checklist and onprem deployment notes + link to quant guide (due 2025-10-15)
Marta: capture kernel version, CUDA/CuDNN and Triton runtime versions from the affected nodes and post in deal thread (due 2025-10-16)
next_steps: Redwood to share layer-sensitivity notebook and reference AWQ configs.
Customer to run narrow bisect (split model into blocks) and send top-5 regressors.
Schedule follow-up triage in one week to review bench results and decide canary rollout strategy.
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-10-14 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~54 minutes
Attendees: Priya Patel (Redwood AE), Evan Chen (Redwood SE), Marta Ruiz (Redwood Infra), Samir Gupta (Monarch Analytics), Tess Huang (Monarch ML Eng), Diego Alvarez (Monarch SRE), Anya K. (Monarch DS)
Links referenced: https://redwood.app/quant-guide (shared), s3://monarch-qa/quant_runs/latest.zip, https://redwood.app/bench-script

[00:00:00] Priya: Hey everyone, thanks for taking the time. quick intro, i'm priya, AE on the account, and evan from the SE team is gonna lead the tech part. do you want to quick run through the symptom?

[00:00:15] Samir: yeah thanks, priya. real quick context — we converted our 13B summarization model using a mix of g p t q and int8, and after deployment onprem we've started seeing a subtle drop in ROUGE and some hallucination on long-context prompts. it's small but visible on our regression tests.

[00:00:33] Evan: okay, thanks. when you say mix — can you share the exact conversion path? g p t q for most layers and int8 for attention?

[00:00:40] Tess: we used GPTQ on FFN and AWQ on attention for speed. config is in the s3 link — we did per-channel int8 on a couple of early layers.

[00:00:52] Evan: got it. one immediate question: are you keeping the KV cache in fp16, or did you quantize it too?

[00:00:58] Samir: we kept the kv in fp16, should be fp16. but the runtime here is an onprem triton-ish stack with a custom kernel set; i'm not 100% sure about the memcpy paths.

[00:01:12] Diego: yeah on the nodes we saw some memcpy spikes when prefix length is > 1024. p95 latency jumps. could be prefetching behavior.

[00:01:25] Evan: ok that suggests two vectors: one is model numeric sensitivity from the quantization, second is runtime I/O and batching interaction. both can make behaviors look like an accuracy regression.

[00:01:39] Anya: our failing tests are mostly long-document summarization and some QA pairs with reasoning chains — seems like attention patterns break.

[00:01:47] Evan: attention is notoriously sensitive. AWQ does great perf but can change outlier behavior for attention weights. GPTQ on FFN usually safe, but mixing can expose cross-layer dynamics.

[00:02:01] Priya: maybe let's list quick hypotheses so we can triage.

[00:02:06] Tess: hypothesis A: AWQ affected attention heads in middle layers causing mis-aligned attention and thus downstream hallucination.

[00:02:15] Samir: B: runtime kernel differences — our triton build might use a slightly different fused attention kernel that behaves differently with int8 paths.

[00:02:23] Marta: C: batching and KV cache eviction timings — with our batching strategy and prefix caching we are seeing KV reorder or stale cache reads on heavy concurrent workloads.

[00:02:36] Evan: good list. for A, we can run a per-layer sensitivity test — quantize one block at a time and measure delta on your eval set. we have a notebook that automates this.

[00:02:48] Priya: i'll share that notebook and an example AWQ config after the call.

[00:02:54] [00:03:00] Samir: when you say per-layer, do you mean freeze everything in fp16 and only quant the target block? that's what you suggest?

[00:03:08] Evan: exactly. blockwise bisect: quantize block index i and keep rest fp16. run evaluation, collect metrics. that isolates which layers drive regressions.

[00:03:20] Tess: is there a recommended default for attention versus ffn? like int8 for ffn, awq for attention? we've seen both recommended.

[00:03:29] Evan: common pattern: FFN -> GPTQ (int8/gptq) tends to preserve quality; attention -> AWQ or mixed 4/8 sometimes better. but it depends — heads with large outliers may need per-channel scaling. AWQ can be tuned with per-head outlier thresholds.

[00:03:45] Diego: any runtime knobs we should be aware of? batch sizes and kv cache op ordering?

[00:03:52] Marta: on our infra, we have continuous batching that coalesces requests, and KV cache writes happen post-token. if a request's prefix shares keys, memcopy contention shows up. maybe we've got a lock contention.

[00:04:05] Evan: yes, and that can manifest as latency increases which triggers client timeouts and partial responses — clients retry and that looks like a functional regression. so must separate pure numeric errors from timing-induced errors.

[00:04:18] Anya: we did isolate a couple examples where the model actually produced a wrong fact, not just timeout errors — those are the concerning ones.

[00:04:26] Evan: ok for that we'll focus on numeric bisect. please run the per-layer test and attach a sample of inputs that reproduce the wrong fact. we'll run it with reference fp16 and with your mixed quant.

[00:04:38] Priya: there's also the possibility that calibration data used during quantization didn't match your production distribution — that causes off-by-some errors in activations. what cal dataset did you use?

[00:04:47] Tess: we used a mix of internal docs and public web scraped news, ~10k tokens.

[00:04:52] Evan: 10k might be okay but needs to match token length distribution. AWQ and GPTQ are both sensitive to long-tail sequences; include longer contexts in calibration.

[00:04:59] Samir: good point. we will include longer docs and re-run cal.

[00:05:05] [00:05:30] Evan: another diagnostic: run a layer norm output comparison in L2 error between fp16 and quantized variants. often a single outlier layer shows 10x higher delta.

[00:05:42] Tess: how do we capture kv cache interaction? is there a way to dump the kv under different quant states?

[00:05:48] Evan: yes, dump the keys/values for a few tokens in fp16 vs quant-run and diff them. if the kv values diverge early, it's a numeric issue; if they match and downstream diverges later, could be runtime or accumulation error.

[00:06:02] Diego: on our side, i can enable extra tracing for memcopy and lock times on the nodes. we'll capture traces during the bench runs.

[00:06:09] Marta: note: our triton build is custom; we had to patch a kernel for low-latency attention. could be regression there. we'll include git sha.

[00:06:18] Priya: perfect, add that to the action items.

[00:06:22] [00:06:40] Samir: one more thing — p99 latency went up only during peak, p50 stable. that suggests batching effects.

[00:06:48] Evan: right. Batching improves throughput but increases tail latency when combined with variable prefix lengths. We recommend adaptive batching window heuristics where short prefixes get micro-batched and long prefixes go on a low-latency path. Redwood runtime supports per-route batching policies.

[00:07:02] Priya: we can propose a temporary mitigation: serve long-context traffic to a fp16-only model pool while we triage quantization. that reduces risk to production.

[00:07:11] Tess: can we do a hybrid pool? like mix per-route pins? we'd like to avoid a full rollback.

[00:07:17] Priya: yes, you can route long-doc traffic to a dedicated pool (fp16) and short responses to quantized pool. it's a routing rule in console. i can send config.

[00:07:26] Evan: also runtime fallback: for requests that exceed an accuracy threshold we can fall back to fp16 at inference time for specific prompt templates (if flagged). that's more heavy-handed but available.

[00:07:36] Anya: about AWQ config — what specific knobs should we tune?

[00:07:41] Evan: key ones: per-head outlier clipping, group size for quantization, and per-channel scaling. AWQ also supports block-wise mixed bits, e.g., 4-bit for non-critical channels and 8-bit for high-sensitivity channels. experiment with larger group sizes first.

[00:07:56] Tess: can GPTQ and AWQ be combined deterministically? our pipeline ran GPTQ for FFN then an AWQ pass for attention. maybe ordering matters.

[00:08:04] Evan: ordering can matter because GPTQ changes the distribution the AWQ pass sees. typical approach: calibrate on fp16 distribution, run GPTQ on FFN blocks, then run AWQ on attention with a fresh calibration pass. also try an interleaved approach if needed.

[00:08:17] [00:08:40] Priya: let's talk about metrics to collect in the bench runs so we can correlate numeric vs infra issues.

[00:08:45] Evan: collect per-layer L2/Linf deltas, per-head attention cosine similarity, token-level perplexity delta, p50/p95/p99 latency with prefix lengths buckets (0-128,129-512,512-2048), KV cache hit/miss stats, memory copy times, and GPU occupancy.

[00:09:05] Diego: i'll add memcopy and lock contention traces. we'll also capture kernel launch times and cuda stream stalls.

[00:09:12] Tess: do you have a script for running these with our onprem runtime?

[00:09:16] Evan: yes, the bench script link we shared — redwood.app/bench-script — has templates for onprem triton stacks. we will fork one for your env and send the command lines.

[00:09:27] Priya: do you want us to spin up a dedicated pool so we don't interfere with prod?

[00:09:31] Samir: yes please, we prefer a dedicated capacity node. we'll schedule a maintenance window for the heavy runs.

[00:09:37] Evan: ok, for ded pooling you'll need to share vpn creds and we'll help configure. Priya will send the infra checklist.

[00:09:44] [00:10:00] Anya: small note — some of the regression examples are reproducible locally with a single prompt. we'll include those in the issue.

[00:10:07] Evan: perfect, that speeds bisecting.

[00:10:12] Tess: on the point of calibration, we should probably try both offline calibrate and online dynamic calibrate runs and compare. any runtime cost for online calibrate?

[00:10:21] Evan: online calibration increases startup time but can adapt to distribution shift. for inference-heavy production it's safer to do offline calibrate with a representative long-tail dataset. but try both for triage.

[00:10:34] [00:10:50] Samir: Curious: any known bugs with AWQ when used with certain fused-attention kernels?

[00:10:55] Marta: briefly — we had a bug in a patched kernel where quantized matmul used an incorrect reorder on 8-bit lanes; that was fixed earlier this year but if you have a custom build it may differ.

[00:11:08] Evan: that's why we asked for kernel SHA. some micro differences cause divergence at long contexts.

[00:11:14] Priya: quick administrative: we'll preserve the meeting recording and the call notes in the deal thread. next meeting in 7 days? does that work?

[00:11:21] Samir: yes next week works.

[00:11:25] [00:11:40] -- fast forward, deeper technical discussion --

[00:11:40] Evan: diving into specifics: for your model the biggest p99 regressors were layers 8-10 and 22-24 per initial diff. that pattern suggests mid-range attention heads. try quantizing only FFN then only attention in separate runs.

[00:12:00] Anya: the delta table you mentioned earlier — what threshold should we consider alarming?

[00:12:06] Evan: heuristic: if layer-wise L2 grows > 3x from baseline or attention cosine < 0.95 for a head, mark as high sensitivity. use those to target per-layer 8-bit fallback.

[00:12:19] Tess: per-layer fallback at runtime — can we configure that in redwood?

[00:12:23] Evan: yes, model config supports overrides per-layer to enforce fp16 for specific blocks during runtime. that requires a model variant but can be automated via rollout.

[00:12:33] Samir: does that add latency overhead?

[00:12:35] Evan: small overhead on model size and cold start but during steady-state tokens it's per-op cost; overall it's preferable to full rollback.

[00:12:42] Diego: regarding batching: we observed p99 spikes correlate with high variance in prefix length. maybe we should segregate request classes by prefix length.

[00:12:50] Evan: yes, segment by prefix length buckets and set max batch windows per bucket. short prefixes get aggressive batching, long prefixes get lower batching and prefetch for KV.

[00:12:59] Marta: also note our CUDA version is 12.1 and we had some deprecation warnings on a fused kernel; might want to check with the kernel vendor.

[00:13:07] Evan: we will map kernel shas to supported CUDA builds. add that to the action list.

[00:13:14] [00:13:30] Tess: question on eval: should we run with sampling temperature 0 or full sampling to capture hallucinations?

[00:13:36] Anya: we run both — deterministic and stochastic. hallucination shows up in both but more frequent with sampling. include both in the bench.

[00:13:44] Evan: good. also capture token-level confidence and logprob shifts. quantization often nudges logits subtly which can make beam searches prefer different tokens.

[00:13:55] Priya: i'll follow up with recommended metric list and the redwood config snippet for routing.

[00:14:02] [00:14:30] -- mid-call side discussion about regression example --

[00:14:30] Samir: here's an example from our failing tests — prompt id 9832 — fp16 output includes the correct company name, quantized run replaces it with a similar name.

[00:14:40] Evan: thanks, we will reproduce. can you also attach the token-level logits for both runs?

[00:14:46] Samir: yes will attach.

[00:14:52] Tess: are there any quick toggles that can reduce risk without a full bisect?

[00:14:57] Evan: quick toggles: increase group size in AWQ, use per-channel scaling on attention, disable quantization for top-k most sensitive heads (we can identify them via the sensitivity notebook).

[00:15:08] Priya: also consider a staged rollout: 5% traffic to quant pool, monitor regression metrics, then scale if safe.

[00:15:17] Diego: question about KV: you recommended keeping KV in fp16 — any reason to try int8 for kv to save memory?

[00:15:24] Evan: kv in int8 can reduce memory but introduces accumulation error over long contexts; we generally avoid quantizing the KV cache for long-context summarization workloads. short chat workloads sometimes can tolerate it.

[00:15:36] Anya: what about fp8 — is that worth trying?

[00:15:39] Evan: fp8 is promising on newer HW — much less quantization noise compared to 4-bit int and good memory saving. but runtime kernel support is still spotty on custom triton builds. if you have HW that supports FP8 (A10X/A100 gen variants), test it, but prioritize INT8/GPTQ/AWQ first because they are more mature in our toolchain.

[00:15:57] [00:16:20] Marta: summarize: we'll collect kernels/sha, cuda versions, triton build, run per-layer bisect, and run bench script with memcopy traces. correct?

[00:16:27] Priya: yes, and redwood will help analyze the per-layer deltas and propose a per-layer fallback config if needed.

[00:16:35] [00:16:50] -- later, walkthrough of proposed bisect notebook --

[00:16:50] Evan: the notebook automates: 1) create N variants each quantizing a single block 2) run eval set 3) compute layerwise metrics 4) output top-k sensitive layers. we'll add a step to capture attention head cosines.

[00:17:05] Tess: will that run on our onprem nodes or do you want to run on a redwood dedicated instance?

[00:17:11] Priya: we prefer you run it on your environment for fidelity; redwood can also run the same notebook in our dedicated pool for a parity check.

[00:17:19] Samir: we'll do both and compare results.

[00:17:24] [00:17:40] -- wrap up: decisions and mitigations --

[00:17:40] Evan: recap of technical plan: 1) per-layer bisect and sensitivity table, 2) calibration dataset expansion to include long-form contexts, 3) run bench script with kernel and memcopy traces, 4) try per-layer fp16 fallback for top sensitive layers, 5) route long-context traffic to fp16 pool during triage.

[00:17:58] Priya: next steps: we'll share the AWQ/GPTQ best-practices doc and the config snippets.

[00:18:04] Tess: ok. thanks — can we get a concrete deadline on the first artifact?

[00:18:09] Evan: i'll upload the per-layer diff script and an example output by friday (2025-10-17).

[00:18:16] Samir: we'll start the bench runs Monday and post results by the 20th.

[00:18:22] Priya: great. anything else from the team?

[00:18:26] Diego: no, we'll get the traces.

[00:18:30] Anya: no other asks.

[00:18:33] Priya: all right thanks everyone — we'll reconvene next week.

[00:18:38] [00:54:00] End of recording
notes: Prioritize per-layer bisect; route long-context traffic to fp16 pool as short-term mitigation.
Collect kernel/sha and runtime build info from nodes and include memcopy lock traces.
Tune AWQ group size and per-channel scaling; consider blockwise mixed bits for sensitive channels.
